name: Obstacle-Avoiding Robot
description: A four-wheel robot that measures distance with an ultrasonic sensor and steers away from obstacles on its own.
objectives: Measure distance with an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor
Drive DC motors through an L298N H-bridge
Write a simple sense-decide-act control loop
prerequisites: Basic Arduino programming (setup/loop, digitalRead/Write, Serial Monitor)
Breadboard wiring and reading a module pin-out
hardware_software: Arduino Uno, ultrasonic sensor, L298N, DIY 4W drive chassis with geared motors, 2 × 18650 cells
Arduino IDE on a laptop
Jumper wires and screwdriver from the lab
steps:
Assemble the chassis
Mount the geared motors and wheels on the DIY 4W drive base; fix the Arduino and L298N with standoffs.

Wire the motor driver
Connect the left and right motor pairs to the L298N outputs and its IN1–IN4 pins to Arduino digital pins.

Mount the sensor
Fix the ultrasonic sensor in its holder at the front; wire TRIG/ECHO to two digital pins.

Program the behaviour
Read the distance every 50 ms; drive forward when clear, otherwise stop, reverse briefly and turn.

Tune
Adjust the stopping distance and turn time on the floor.
outcome: The robot drives around a room and turns away before touching walls or boxes.
testing: Print distances to the Serial Monitor and compare with a ruler at 10, 20 and 50 cm
Run each motor direction on its own with the wheels lifted
Place boxes in its path and confirm it stops before contact
safety: Insert 18650 cells with the correct polarity, never short them, and charge them only with the lab charger.
Lift the wheels off the bench when testing motors.
Disconnect power before changing any wiring.
extensions: Add a servo to sweep the sensor and choose the clearer side
Use PWM speed control for smoother turns

components.note: Chassis kit with geared motors – check the kit contents

image_alt: Four-wheel robot chassis with an Arduino, an L298N motor driver and an ultrasonic sensor at the front facing an obstacle

name: Bluetooth-Controlled Robot
description: Drive a robot car from a phone: an HC-05 Bluetooth module receives commands and the Arduino turns them into motor movement.
objectives: Map received characters to motor commands
Control motor direction and speed with an L298N
prerequisites: Basic Arduino programming (setup/loop, digitalRead/Write, Serial Monitor)
Breadboard wiring and reading a module pin-out
hardware_software: Arduino Uno, HC-05, L298N, DIY 4W drive chassis, 2 × 18650 cells
Arduino IDE on a laptop
Android phone with a Bluetooth serial controller app (student’s own)
steps:
Assemble the drive base
Fit motors, wheels, Arduino and L298N on the DIY 4W drive chassis.

Connect the HC-05
HC-05 TX → Arduino RX (via SoftwareSerial pins); Arduino TX → HC-05 RX through a 1 kΩ/2 kΩ divider (3.3 V logic).

Define commands
F, B, L, R, S for forward, back, left, right, stop; parse them in loop().

Pair and drive
Pair the phone (default PIN 1234), connect from the app and test each command.
outcome: The robot responds to phone buttons within a fraction of a second and stops when commanded.
testing: Send commands from a serial terminal app and watch the Serial Monitor echo
Check that every command moves the correct wheels
Confirm the robot stops if the app sends S
safety: Insert 18650 cells with the correct polarity, never short them, and charge them only with the lab charger.
Never connect the HC-05 RX pin directly to 5 V logic – use the divider.
Test at low speed in an open area.
extensions: Add a fail-safe stop when no command arrives for one second
Add speed levels with PWM
image_alt: Robot car with an HC-05 Bluetooth module wirelessly linked to a smartphone controller

name: Line-Following Robot
description: A two-wheel robot that follows a black line on the floor using two IR reflectance sensors.
objectives: Tune a simple bang-bang or proportional controller
prerequisites: Basic Arduino programming (setup/loop, digitalRead/Write, Serial Monitor)
Breadboard wiring and reading a module pin-out
hardware_software: Arduino Uno, 2 IR sensor modules, L298N, DIY 2W drive chassis, 2 × 18650 cells
Arduino IDE on a laptop
steps:
Build the base
Assemble the DIY 2W drive with its castor wheel and mount the electronics.

Fit the sensors
Mount two IR modules 1–2 cm above the floor, either side of the line; set each threshold with its potentiometer.

Wire and program
If the left sensor sees black, turn left; if the right sees black, turn right; otherwise go straight.

Make a track
Tape a closed loop with gentle curves on a light floor.
outcome: The robot completes laps of the taped track without losing the line.
testing: Check each sensor’s LED switches over black tape and white floor
Run straight sections first, then curves
Time three laps and note any departures
safety: Insert 18650 cells with the correct polarity, never short them, and charge them only with the lab charger.
Disconnect power before changing any wiring.
extensions: Use more IR sensors and a PID controller
Add junction detection for a maze
image_alt: Two-wheel robot with IR sensors underneath following a black line track
external: Black insulating tape for the track

name: Servo-Based Robotic Arm
description: Program the lab’s 6-DoF mini arm joint by joint, then combine moves into a basic pick-and-place routine.
objectives: Understand joint angles and workspace limits
prerequisites: Basic Arduino programming (setup/loop, digitalRead/Write, Serial Monitor)
Basic geometry (angles)
hardware_software: 6 DoF Mini Arm (lab use), Arduino Uno, external 5–6 V supply for the servos
Arduino IDE on a laptop with the Servo library
steps:
Inspect the arm
Identify each joint’s servo and its safe angle range; check whether the arm has its own controller board.

Power safely
Power the servos from the separate supply, sharing ground with the Arduino.

Move one joint at a time
Write a sketch that moves each servo slowly between limits.

Record poses
Store joint angles for home, reach, grip and lift.

Sequence
Interpolate between poses to pick up a small foam block.
outcome: The arm moves smoothly between stored poses and repeats a simple pick-and-place.
testing: Verify each joint stays within its mechanical limits
Repeat the pick-and-place ten times and count successes
safety: Keep hands clear of the arm while it moves.
Never power several servos from the Arduino 5 V pin.
This equipment is for use inside the lab only.
extensions: Control the arm from a joystick or potentiometers
Add inverse kinematics for target positions

components.note: Servo power supply – check voltage before use

image_alt: Six-degree-of-freedom desktop robotic arm with servo joints lifting a small block
verification: Confirm whether the 6 DoF Mini Arm includes its own servo controller and the voltage its servos need.

name: Omnidirectional Robot
description: Explore holonomic motion on the lab’s Smorphi mecanum platform: strafing, rotating in place and following paths.
objectives: Command forward, sideways and rotational velocities
prerequisites: Programming experience in C++ or Python
Vectors and basic trigonometry
hardware_software: Smorphi with AI features (lab use)
Smorphi programming environment supplied with the platform
Laptop
steps:
Read the platform guide
Learn how Smorphi is powered, charged and programmed, and its speed limits.

Basic motions
Command forward, sideways and rotate-in-place motions and observe the wheels.

Kinematics
Write a function that converts (vx, vy, ω) to the four wheel speeds.

Path following
Drive a square without changing heading, then a circle while facing the centre.
outcome: The robot moves in any direction without turning first and follows a planned square path.
testing: Measure drift after a 1 m sideways move
Repeat the square path three times and compare end positions
safety: Run in a clear, enclosed area at low speed.
Follow the platform’s charging instructions.
This equipment is for use inside the lab only.
extensions: Add obstacle avoidance with the platform’s sensors
Compare with the Twin Bot drive system
image_alt: Modular mecanum-wheel robot platform moving sideways with motion arrows

name: 3D-Printed Robot Chassis
description: Design a custom robot chassis in CAD, print it on the lab’s 3D printer and build a working robot on it.
objectives: Integrate motors, driver and sensor on a custom frame
prerequisites: Basic CAD (Fusion 360, Tinkercad or FreeCAD)
Basic Arduino programming (setup/loop, digitalRead/Write, Serial Monitor)
hardware_software: 3D printer (lab use), Arduino Uno, L298N, 2 small DC motors, ultrasonic sensor, 18650 cells
CAD software and a slicer (e.g. Cura)
steps:
Measure
Measure motors, boards and battery holder; plan mounting holes.

Design
Model a base plate with motor clamps, standoffs and a sensor mount.

Print
Slice with suitable infill and supports; print with staff supervision.

Assemble
Fit motors, wheels, electronics and wiring with screws from the screw box.

Test drive
Load a simple drive or obstacle-avoiding sketch.
outcome: A printed chassis that carries the electronics securely and drives without flexing.
testing: Check every part fits before final assembly
Drive for five minutes and inspect for cracks or loose mounts
safety: The printer nozzle and bed are hot – do not touch during or just after printing.
Only start prints with staff permission.
Insert 18650 cells with the correct polarity, never short them, and charge them only with the lab charger.
extensions: Add a battery compartment with a hinged lid
Design snap-fit mounts instead of screws
image_alt: 3D printer printing a robot chassis plate next to motors and an Arduino
external: Wheels compatible with the DC motor shafts

name: IoT Smart Home Automation
description: Control four low-voltage loads from a web page served by an ESP32, with a PIR sensor for automatic lighting.
objectives: Serve a web interface from an ESP32
Switch loads with an opto-isolated relay module
prerequisites: Arduino IDE with ESP32 board support
Basic HTML
Breadboard wiring and reading a module pin-out
hardware_software: ESP32, 4-channel relay module, PIR sensor, LEDs as stand-in loads
Arduino IDE (ESP32 core), Wi-Fi network
steps:
Wire the relay board
Connect IN1–IN4 to ESP32 GPIOs; power the relay side from 5 V with common ground.

Add loads
Use LEDs with resistors as the four “appliances”.

Build the web server
Serve a page with four toggle buttons that call /relay?ch=n&on=1.

Add automation
Turn channel 1 on for 30 s when the PIR detects motion.
outcome: A phone on the same Wi-Fi can switch four outputs, and the light turns on automatically when someone walks past.
testing: Toggle each channel from the page and confirm the relay click and LED
Walk past the PIR and time the automatic light
safety: Use only low-voltage (≤12 V) loads – do not connect mains to the relays.
Disconnect power before changing any wiring.
extensions: Add MQTT and a cloud dashboard
Schedule loads by time of day
image_alt: ESP32 board connected to a four-channel relay module controlling lights from a phone over Wi-Fi

name: Smart Irrigation System
description: Water a plant only when it needs it: a soil-moisture sensor decides when a relay switches a small pump on.
objectives: Switch a pump safely through a relay
prerequisites: Basic Arduino programming (setup/loop, digitalRead/Write, Serial Monitor)
hardware_software: Arduino Uno, soil moisture sensor, 1-channel relay
Small 5 V submersible pump with tubing (not stocked)
Arduino IDE on a laptop
steps:
Calibrate
Record sensor readings in dry soil and freshly watered soil.

Wire
Sensor to A0; relay IN to a digital pin; pump powered through the relay contacts.

Program
Pump on below the dry threshold, off above the wet threshold (hysteresis).

Install
Place the probe near the roots and route the tube to the pot.
outcome: The pump runs only when the soil is dry and stops once it is moist.
testing: Test with a cup of dry and wet soil
Confirm the pump cannot run longer than a maximum time
safety: Keep the electronics away from water; mount them above the pot.
Use a low-voltage pump only.
extensions: Log moisture to an SD card or the cloud
Add a rain sensor to skip watering
image_alt: Potted plant with a soil moisture probe, an Arduino and a relay driving a small water pump
external: Small 5 V water pump and tubing

name: Environmental Monitoring Station
description: Measure temperature and air quality with an ESP32 and show the readings on a web page.
objectives: Read analogue sensors with the ESP32 ADC
prerequisites: Arduino IDE with ESP32 board support
Breadboard wiring and reading a module pin-out
hardware_software: ESP32, analogue temperature sensor, MQ-series gas sensor
Arduino IDE (ESP32 core), Wi-Fi
steps:
Wire sensors
Temperature sensor to an ADC pin; gas sensor AO to another ADC pin (scale to 3.3 V).

Warm up
Let the MQ sensor heat for several minutes before taking readings.

Convert
Turn temperature voltage into °C; record gas readings as relative values.

Serve
Show live values on a web page that refreshes every few seconds.
outcome: A web page shows the room temperature and a relative air-quality reading that changes with conditions.
testing: Compare temperature with a reference thermometer
Check the gas reading rises with hand-sanitiser vapour nearby
safety: The MQ sensor heater gets hot – do not touch it.
Never test with flammable gases.
extensions: Add humidity sensing and charts
Push data to a cloud service
image_alt: ESP32 weather station with temperature and gas sensors sending readings to a dashboard

name: RFID-Based Access Control
description: Grant or deny entry with RFID cards: authorised tags open a servo latch and the LCD shows who was admitted.
objectives: Read RFID tag UIDs over SPI
Drive a servo latch and LCD feedback
prerequisites: Basic Arduino programming (setup/loop, digitalRead/Write, Serial Monitor)
Arrays and string comparison
hardware_software: Arduino Uno, RFID reader with tags, SG90 servo, 16×2 LCD with I2C adapter, LEDs
Arduino IDE on a laptop with MFRC522 and LiquidCrystal_I2C libraries
steps:
Read tags
Wire the RFID reader (3.3 V) and print each tag’s UID.

Allow-list
Store approved UIDs; compare each scan.

Feedback
Green LED + “Access granted” or red LED + “Denied” on the LCD.

Latch
Rotate the servo to unlock for three seconds, then relock.
outcome: Authorised cards unlock the latch; unknown cards are refused and shown on screen.
testing: Scan authorised and unauthorised tags ten times each
Confirm the latch always relocks
safety: Power the RFID reader from 3.3 V, not 5 V.
Disconnect power before changing any wiring.
extensions: Log access with timestamps (add the RTC module)
Add an admin card that enrols new tags
image_alt: RFID card reader next to a door latch with an LCD showing access granted

name: GSM-Based Alert System
description: Send an SMS when a motion sensor is triggered, using a SIM800L GSM module.
objectives: Use AT commands to control a GSM modem
prerequisites: Basic Arduino programming (setup/loop, digitalRead/Write, Serial Monitor)
Serial communication
hardware_software: Arduino Uno, SIM800L, PIR sensor, DC buck supply set to about 4 V
Active SIM card with SMS (not stocked)
Arduino IDE on a laptop
steps:
Power
Set the buck converter to about 4.0 V and connect it to the SIM800L with a short, thick lead.

Talk to the modem
Use SoftwareSerial to send AT, AT+CSQ and AT+CREG? and read the replies.

Send an SMS
Use AT+CMGF=1 and AT+CMGS to send a test message.

Trigger
Send one alert when the PIR fires, then wait before the next.
outcome: A phone receives an SMS within seconds of motion being detected.
testing: Check signal quality (AT+CSQ) before testing
Trigger the PIR and time SMS delivery
Confirm repeated motion does not flood messages
safety: The SIM800L draws current spikes – use the buck supply, not the Arduino 5 V pin.
Use your own SIM and agree costs before testing.
extensions: Reply to SMS commands such as STATUS
Add a GPS location to alerts
image_alt: SIM800L GSM module wired to an Arduino sending an SMS alert to a phone
external: Active SIM card with SMS credit

name: Fire and Flame Detection Alarm
description: Sound a buzzer and flash an LED when an IR flame sensor detects a flame.
prerequisites: Basic Arduino programming (setup/loop, digitalRead/Write, Serial Monitor)
hardware_software: Arduino Uno, flame sensor module, piezo buzzer, LEDs
Arduino IDE on a laptop
steps:
Wire
Flame sensor DO/AO to Arduino; buzzer and LEDs to outputs.

Calibrate
Adjust the module potentiometer so room light does not trigger it.

Program
On detection, sound the buzzer and flash the red LED until reset.
outcome: The alarm sounds within a second when a small flame is held in front of the sensor.
testing: Test with a lighter flame at 20, 50 and 100 cm under supervision
Check sunlight or lamps do not cause false alarms
safety: Flame tests only with staff present, away from paper and with no flammable materials nearby.
This is a teaching model, not a certified fire alarm.
extensions: Add the GSM module to send an SMS alert
Add a smoke/gas sensor
image_alt: Flame sensor module detecting a candle flame with a buzzer and red warning LED

name: Smart Walking Stick
description: An assistive walking stick that warns of obstacles ahead with a buzzer and vibration.
objectives: Give graded feedback (faster beeps when closer)
Package electronics for a wearable/handheld device
prerequisites: Basic Arduino programming (setup/loop, digitalRead/Write, Serial Monitor)
Breadboard wiring and reading a module pin-out
hardware_software: Walking stick, Arduino Nano, ultrasonic sensor, buzzer, vibration motor, 18650 cells
Arduino IDE on a laptop
steps:
Mount
Fix the ultrasonic sensor near the bottom of the stick, angled slightly forward.

Wire
Nano, buzzer and vibration motor (through a transistor) in a small enclosure near the handle.

Program
Beep and vibrate faster as obstacles get closer than 1 m.

Package
Secure wires along the stick and make the battery easy to remove.
outcome: Walking towards a wall, the user feels and hears increasingly urgent warnings.
testing: Measure warning distance against a tape measure
Walk a corridor with obstacles and note any missed objects
safety: Insert 18650 cells with the correct polarity, never short them, and charge them only with the lab charger.
Prototype only – not a replacement for a certified mobility aid.
extensions: Add a second sensor for head-height obstacles
Add a fall-detection accelerometer
image_alt: Walking stick fitted with an ultrasonic sensor and a handle unit that buzzes near obstacles

name: Fingerprint-Based Attendance System
description: Enrol fingerprints and mark attendance with a timestamp shown on an LCD.
objectives: Enrol and match fingerprints with an optical sensor
prerequisites: Basic Arduino programming (setup/loop, digitalRead/Write, Serial Monitor)
Serial communication
hardware_software: Arduino Uno, fingerprint reader, 16×2 LCD with I2C adapter, DS3231 RTC
Arduino IDE on a laptop with Adafruit Fingerprint and RTClib libraries
steps:
Enrol
Run the library’s enrol example to store a few test fingerprints.

Match
On a successful match, look up the student ID.

Timestamp
Read the RTC and show “ID 3 – 09:12 present” on the LCD.

Log
Print each record over serial (or to an SD card as an extension).
outcome: Enrolled users are recognised and their attendance time is displayed and logged.
testing: Test each enrolled finger five times and record false rejects
Try an unenrolled finger and confirm it is refused
safety: Use only volunteers’ test prints and delete them afterwards – do not store real biometric data.
Disconnect power before changing any wiring.
extensions: Upload records to a spreadsheet over Wi-Fi
Add duplicate-scan protection
image_alt: Optical fingerprint sensor with an LCD showing an attendance record

name: Heart Rate Monitoring Prototype
description: Display pulse readings from a finger-clip heart-rate sensor on an LCD, for learning about biosignals.
objectives: Detect beats and compute beats per minute
prerequisites: Basic Arduino programming (setup/loop, digitalRead/Write, Serial Monitor)
Basic signal concepts (sampling, noise)
hardware_software: Arduino Uno, heart rate monitor module, 16×2 LCD with I2C adapter
Arduino IDE on a laptop and Serial Plotter
steps:
Wire
Sensor signal to A0; LCD on I2C.

Visualise
Plot raw readings in the Serial Plotter while resting a fingertip on the sensor.

Detect beats
Find peaks above an adaptive threshold and time the gap between them.

Display
Show a smoothed BPM value on the LCD.
outcome: The LCD shows a stable pulse reading that is close to a manual count.
testing: Compare with a 30-second manual pulse count
Check readings with the finger still and slightly moving
safety: For education only – never use it for medical decisions.
Use only the low-voltage sensor; no electrodes on the chest.
extensions: Add the wireless logger (project 38)
Detect irregular intervals
image_alt: Finger on a pulse sensor with a heartbeat waveform and BPM reading on an LCD

name: Water Turbidity Monitoring
description: Measure how cloudy water samples are with a turbidity sensor and show a relative reading.
prerequisites: Basic Arduino programming (setup/loop, digitalRead/Write, Serial Monitor)
hardware_software: Arduino Uno, turbidity sensor, 16×2 LCD with I2C adapter
Clear containers and water samples (not stocked)
Arduino IDE on a laptop
steps:
Wire
Sensor analogue output to A0; LCD on I2C.

Calibrate
Record readings for clean water and for water with increasing amounts of clay or milk.

Map
Convert readings into a relative 0–100 cloudiness scale.

Display
Show the value and a Clear/Cloudy/Dirty label.
outcome: Different samples give clearly different, repeatable readings.
testing: Measure each sample three times and compare spread
Check the sensor head is dried between samples
safety: Keep the electronics dry; only the probe tip goes in water.
Do not drink test samples.
extensions: Log readings over time for a water tank
Combine with a temperature sensor
image_alt: Turbidity probe dipped in a beaker of cloudy water with readings on a display

name: AI Object Detection
description: Run a pretrained object-detection model on the Jetson Nano with the Intel depth camera and draw labelled boxes in real time.
prerequisites: Python and Linux command line
Basic machine-learning concepts
hardware_software: Jetson Nano (lab use), Intel depth camera, monitor/keyboard
JetPack OS image, jetson-inference or similar, Python, librealsense
steps:
Prepare
Check the Jetson’s power supply and SD-card image with staff.

Camera
Connect the Intel camera and confirm it streams.

Model
Run a pretrained SSD/YOLO model and display boxes and labels.

Evaluate
Measure frames per second and test on lab objects.
outcome: The screen shows live video with correctly labelled boxes around common objects.
testing: Record FPS at two input resolutions
Count correct/incorrect detections on 20 test objects
safety: The Jetson heatsink gets hot – keep the fan clear.
Lab use only; shut down properly before unplugging.
extensions: Use depth to report each object’s distance
Train on a custom dataset of lab components
image_alt: Jetson Nano board with a camera showing object-detection boxes on a screen
verification: Confirm the Jetson Nano power supply and OS image, and that this Intel depth camera model works with librealsense on the Jetson.

name: Stereo Vision and Depth Mapping
description: Use the ZED-2 stereo camera kit to compute depth maps and 3D point clouds of the lab.
objectives: Use a vendor SDK to capture depth
prerequisites: Python or C++
Basic linear algebra
hardware_software: ZED-2 Stereolabs Xavier NX kit (lab use)
ZED SDK, Python API, monitor
steps:
Start
Boot the Xavier NX kit and launch the ZED Explorer to confirm the camera works.

Depth
Capture a depth map and display it as a colour image.

Measure
Read the distance at chosen pixels and compare with a tape measure.

Point cloud
Export and view a point cloud of a scene.
outcome: Depth maps and a 3D point cloud of the lab, with measured distances within a few centimetres.
testing: Compare measured distances at 0.5, 1 and 2 m
Check accuracy on shiny and dark surfaces
safety: Lab use only; handle the camera by its body, not the lenses.
Shut the kit down properly before disconnecting power.
extensions: Detect people and report their 3D positions
Build a simple 3D reconstruction
image_alt: ZED-2 stereo camera with a colourful depth map of a room

name: LiDAR-Based Mapping and Navigation
description: Build a 2D map of a room with the lab’s LiDAR and a ROS SLAM package, then plan paths on it.
objectives: Run a SLAM algorithm to build a map
Understand occupancy grids and path planning
prerequisites: Linux and ROS basics
Python or C++
hardware_software: 2D LiDAR sensor and mini PC (lab use)
ROS with the LiDAR’s driver, SLAM toolbox/gmapping, RViz
steps:
Identify
Find the LiDAR model and install its ROS driver on the mini PC.

Scan
Visualise live scans in RViz.

Map
Carry or slowly move the sensor around a room while SLAM builds the map.

Plan
Save the map and plan a path between two points.
outcome: A saved occupancy-grid map that matches the room layout.
testing: Compare map dimensions with measured room size
Rebuild the map twice and compare
safety: Most 2D LiDARs are Class 1 lasers, but never look into the emitter.
Lab use only.
extensions: Mount on the Twin Bot for autonomous navigation (project 40)
Detect moving people in scans
image_alt: Spinning 2D LiDAR sensor with laser scan lines building a floor-plan map
verification: Confirm the LiDAR model, its connection (USB/serial) and an available ROS driver.

name: Drone Telemetry and Control
description: Explore the C-DAC drone kit’s flight controller: read telemetry, configure it and understand control loops – flight only after staff approval.
objectives: Read telemetry (attitude, battery, GPS) from a flight controller
prerequisites: Electronics and programming experience
Completion of the lab’s drone safety briefing
hardware_software: C-DAC drone kit with its supplied controller and software (lab use)
Ground-control software supplied with the kit
steps:
Inventory the kit
With staff, list what the kit contains and read its manuals.

Bench setup
With propellers removed, connect the flight controller to the ground-control software.

Telemetry
Record attitude and battery readings while tilting the frame by hand.

Review
Study the PID settings; any flight test only in an approved area with staff present.
outcome: Live telemetry from the flight controller and a written understanding of its control settings.
testing: Tilt the frame and confirm the attitude display follows
Check battery voltage readings against a meter
safety: Propellers OFF for all bench work.
No flying without staff approval, an approved area and applicable permissions.
Handle LiPo batteries per the kit instructions.
extensions: Log telemetry and plot it after a supervised flight
Study failsafe settings
image_alt: Quadcopter drone kit with telemetry data shown on a ground-control screen
verification: Verify the kit contents, its software and the safety and permission requirements before any flight.

name: Smart Parking Assistant
description: Help a driver park: an ultrasonic sensor lights green, yellow and red LEDs and beeps as a car gets closer.
prerequisites: Basic Arduino programming (setup/loop, digitalRead/Write, Serial Monitor)
hardware_software: Arduino Uno, ultrasonic sensor, LEDs, buzzer
Arduino IDE on a laptop
steps:
Wire
Ultrasonic sensor, three LEDs with resistors and a buzzer.

Bands
Green above 50 cm, yellow 20–50 cm, red and fast beeping below 20 cm.

Smooth
Average several readings to avoid flicker.
outcome: A toy car approaching the sensor changes the lights and beeps at the right distances.
testing: Check each band with a ruler
Move an object slowly and confirm no flicker between bands
safety: Disconnect power before changing any wiring.
extensions: Show the distance on an LCD
Count free parking slots with several sensors
image_alt: Car approaching a wall-mounted ultrasonic sensor with green, yellow and red distance lights

name: Automatic Door Prototype
description: A model door that opens with a servo when a PIR sensor detects someone approaching, and closes after a delay.
prerequisites: Basic Arduino programming (setup/loop, digitalRead/Write, Serial Monitor)
hardware_software: Arduino Uno, PIR sensor, SG90 servo
Cardboard or foam-board door model (not stocked)
Arduino IDE on a laptop
steps:
Build the model
Make a small door on a hinge with the servo horn attached.

Wire
PIR output to a digital pin; servo signal to a PWM pin.

Program
States: closed → opening → open (5 s) → closing; restart the timer if motion continues.
outcome: The model door opens when a hand approaches and closes a few seconds after it leaves.
testing: Approach from different angles and distances
Check the door never closes while motion continues
safety: Keep fingers clear of the hinge while the servo moves.
Disconnect power before changing any wiring.
extensions: Add RFID so only authorised cards open it
Count people entering
image_alt: Model sliding door with a motion sensor above it and a servo opening it

name: Gas Leakage Alert
description: Raise an alarm when an MQ-series gas sensor reading crosses a set threshold.
objectives: Use a heated MQ gas sensor
prerequisites: Basic Arduino programming (setup/loop, digitalRead/Write, Serial Monitor)
hardware_software: Arduino Uno, MQ-series gas sensor, buzzer, LEDs
Arduino IDE on a laptop
steps:
Wire
Sensor AO to A0; buzzer and LEDs to outputs.

Warm up
Run the sensor for several minutes and note the clean-air reading.

Threshold
Set an alarm level well above clean air.

Alarm
Red LED and buzzer until the reading falls back, then green.
outcome: Exposing the sensor to a little sanitiser vapour triggers the alarm, which clears in clean air.
testing: Log clean-air readings for five minutes
Test with sanitiser vapour (never fuel gas)
safety: Never release LPG, butane or other flammable gas to test.
The sensor heater is hot.
Teaching model only – not a certified gas detector.
extensions: Send an SMS with the GSM module
Switch an exhaust fan with a relay
image_alt: MQ gas sensor module with a warning buzzer and red alert LED

name: Temperature-Controlled Fan
description: Run a small DC fan faster as the temperature rises, using PWM through a MOSFET module.
objectives: Drive a motor with PWM and a MOSFET
prerequisites: Basic Arduino programming (setup/loop, digitalRead/Write, Serial Monitor)
Breadboard wiring and reading a module pin-out
hardware_software: Arduino Uno, temperature sensor, IRF520 MOSFET module, small DC motor, 1N4007 diode, 18650 cells
Small propeller/fan blade for the motor (not stocked)
Arduino IDE on a laptop
steps:
Wire the sensor
Temperature sensor output to A0; convert to °C.

Wire the motor
